research.title: Evidence Sensitivity in Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering
bullets: Designed controlled experiments varying passage relevance, evidence ordering, and distractor content to examine answer grounding in retrieval-augmented question answering.
Analyzed answer correctness and citation support across retrieval conditions, separating failures caused by missing evidence from failures to use available evidence.

research.title: Confidence Calibration for Cross-Domain Sentiment Classification
bullets: Designed cross-domain evaluation protocols comparing temperature scaling and uncalibrated predictions for sentiment classifiers under shifts in vocabulary and review style.
Analyzed reliability diagrams, calibration error, and selective prediction behavior, examining how confidence estimates changed across domains and ambiguous sentiment examples.

research.title: Negation and Lexical Overlap in Natural Language Inference
bullets: Designed matched evaluation sets that varied negation placement and lexical overlap while preserving controlled relationships between premises and hypotheses.
Analyzed prediction changes across sentence encoders and transformer classifiers, categorizing errors by negation scope, lexical cues, and inference label.

projects.title: Comparative Evaluation of Named Entity Tagging Models
bullets: Implemented conditional random field and bidirectional recurrent tagging baselines with consistent tokenization, label encoding, and data splits for named entity recognition.
Compared entity-level precision, recall, and boundary errors, examining performance differences for rare entities, ambiguous names, and multiword mentions.

projects.title: Sparse and Contextual Representations for Topic Classification
bullets: Implemented topic classifiers using term frequency–inverse document frequency features and pooled transformer embeddings, applying identical training partitions and label preprocessing.
Compared macro-averaged classification metrics and confusion patterns, inspecting errors associated with short documents, overlapping topics, and domain-specific terminology.
